author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A 1969 novel in which a team of anti-psychic 'inertials' survives a bomb blast only to find their world sliding backward through time and decaying around them, sustained fitfully by a mysterious spray-can product called Ubik—Dick's central meditation on entropy, half-life, and a divine force hidden in commercial trash.
page_summary:
Glen Runciter runs a firm of 'inertials' who neutralize telepaths; when a sabotage explosion on the Moon apparently kills him, his team retreats to have him preserved in 'half-life,' the suspended state in which the dead can still be spoken to. But then reality begins to run down: cigarettes crumble, coins go obsolete, appliances regress to older models, and the world slips toward 1939. Messages from Runciter appear in the decay—on graffiti, on matchbooks, in television commercials—advertising Ubik, a spray that briefly halts the collapse, while a predatory consciousness named Jory feeds on the trapped survivors. Who is truly dead, and who is sustaining the world, becomes the novel's shifting mystery.

Dick stages reality breakdown as entropy made tactile: existence itself becomes a product requiring constant maintenance and payment, decaying the moment the maintenance fails. Yet the saving force arrives at the bottom, through kipple and cheap advertising—the chapter epigraphs pitch Ubik as beer, coffee, a hangover cure, until the final one drops the mask ('I am Ubik. Before the universe was, I am'). After 1974, Dick came to read his own book as accidental scripture, glossing Ubik as the immanent Holy Spirit and Runciter as the Logos breaking into a dying world (his own later self-interpretation, not the novel's stated claim).

Ubik is one of Dick's essential novels, routinely ranked among his best, and the purest fusion of his two obsessions: the commercial dystopia as a system of control and the metaphysical instability of reality itself.

biography_events.event: A profound LSD trip in 1964 ("about 350 mices"), where he "hit the Dies Irae."
Publishes the novel Ubik exploring themes of entropy and false realities
In 1970, PKD wrote 4 letters to Sandra Miesel, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of the science-fiction community, money and royalty problems, and family and relationship strain.

In 1973, PKD wrote 7 letters to Diane Cleaver, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of the science-fiction community, family and relationship strain, and publishing and career pressures.
Seeing the "Eye of Horus" as the judge of the 1974 revolution.
The 1974 "second pass" regarding the Xerox letter and Nixon's fall.
The 1974 induction of "inner anamnesis" by the Golden Fish sign.
The 2-74 "withdrawal of assent" which caused 1974 California to disappear.
